Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.

Groups naturally give rise to several actions on themselves.
Right action
$ xg=xg $
Left action
$ gx=gx $

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Relations
A relation between sets \(A\) and \(B\) is a subset \(R \subset A \times B\).
If \(R \subset X \times X\), then \(R\) is a relation on \(X\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Functions
A function \(f\) from a set \(A\) to a set \(B\) is a relation from \(A\) to \(B\) such that each \(a \in A\) is related to exactly one element \(b \in B\).
We write
\[
f:A\to B
\]

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Functions
We write \(f(a)=b\) if \(b\) is the unique element of \(B\) associated with \(a\).

\(A\) is the domain of \(f\).
\(B\) is the range or codomain of \(f\).
The set \[
f(A)=\{f(a):a\in A\}
\] is the image of \(f\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Surjective Functions
Let \(f:A\to B\) be a function.
The function \(f\) is onto or surjective if every element in \(B\) is the image of some element in \(A\).
That is, for every \(b\in B\), there exists an \(a\in A\) such that \(f(a)=b\).
Sometimes you will this way of expressing onto functions, \(f(A)=B\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
One-to-One Functions
Let \(f:A\to B\) be a function.
The function \(f\) is one-to-one or injective if \(f(a_1)=f(a_2)\) implies \(a_1=a_2\).
That is each element in the image comes from a unique element in the domain.

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Definition of Equivalence Relation
Let \(R \subset X \times X\) be a relation on \(X\).
The relation \(R\) is an equivalence relation when:

Reflexive: \((x,x) \in R\) for all \(x \in X\).
Symmetric: If \((x,y) \in R\), then \((y,x) \in R\).
Transitive: If \((x,y) \in R\) and \((y,z) \in R\), then \((x,z) \in R\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

Equivalence Classes
Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\).
For \(x\in X\), the equivalence class of \(x\) is \([x]=\{y\in X:y\sim x\}\).
Equivalence classes have two important properties:

\([x]=[y]\), or
\([x]\cap[y]=\emptyset\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Equivalence Classes Partition sets
Thus, the equivalence classes of \(X\) form a partition of \(X\):
\[
X=\bigcup_{x\in X}[x].
\]
Every element of \(X\) belongs to exactly one equivalence class.

Caution: Functions on Equivalence Classes
Suppose we want to define a function on equivalence classes by
\(f([x]) = \text{some expression involving } x\).
Be careful! An equivalence class can have many different representatives.

To show that \(f\) is well-defined, we must check that the value of \(f([x])\) does not depend on the choice of representative.
That is, we need to prove:

If \(x \sim y\), then \(f([x])=f([y])\).



Defining a rule is not enough — check that it is well-defined!

section: Well Ordering of the Natural Numbers
text:
Well Ordering of the Natural Numbers
A set \(S\) is well-ordered if every nonempty subset of \(S\) contains a least element.
Principle of Well-Ordering. Every nonempty subset of the natural numbers is well-ordered.
In this class the natural numbers are \(\mathbb{N}=\{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
What about the integers?
The integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) are not well-ordered.
For example,
\[
\{\ldots,-4,-3,-2,-1\}
\]
has no least element.

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm
Division Algorithm. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers, with \(b>0\). Then there exist unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(a=bq+r\) where \(0\leq r<b\).
The proof has three parts:

Existence: Show that \(q\) and \(r\) exist.
\(0\leq r<b\)
Uniqueness: Show that no other \(q\) and \(r\) can satisfy these conditions.

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Existence
Let \(S=\{a-bk:k\in\mathbb Z\text{ and }a-bk\geq 0\}.\) If \(0\in S\), then \(b\) divides \(a\), and we can let
\[
q=\frac{a}{b}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
r=0.
\]
Suppose \(0\notin S\). We first show that \(S\) is nonempty. If \(a>0\), then \(a-b\cdot 0\in S\). If \(a<0\), then \(a-b(2a)=a(1-2b)\in S\) Thus \(S\neq\varnothing\).

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Existence
By the Principle of Well-Ordering, \(S\) has a smallest member, say
\[
r=a-bq.
\]
Therefore,
\[
a=bq+r
\]
and \(r\geq 0\).
We now show that \(r<b\).
Suppose that \(r>b\). Then
\[
a-b(q+1)=a-bq-b=r-b>0.
\]
Thus \(a-b(q+1)\in S\), but
\[
a-b(q+1)<a-bq=r,
\]
contradicting the fact that \(r\) is the smallest member of \(S\).
Hence \(r\leq b\). Since \(0\notin S\), \(r\neq b\), and therefore
\[
0\leq r<b.
\]

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Uniqueness
Suppose there exist integers \(r,r',q,q'\) such that
\[
a=bq+r,\qquad 0\leq r<b
\]
and
\[
a=bq'+r',\qquad 0\leq r'<b.
\]
Then
\[
bq+r=bq'+r'.
\]
Assume that \(r'\geq r\). Then
\[
b(q-q')=r'-r.
\]
Therefore \(b\) divides \(r'-r\), but
\[
0\leq r'-r\leq r'<b.
\]
This is possible only if
\[
r'-r=0.
\]
Hence \(r=r'\) and \(q=q'\).

Invertible Function Theorem
Theorem 1.2.20.
A mapping is invertible if and only if it is both one-to-one and onto.

In other words,
\[
f \text{ is invertible}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f \text{ is injective and surjective}.
\]

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Composition of Mappings
Theorem 1.2.15.
Let \(f:A\to B\), \(g:B\to C\), and \(h:C\to D\). Then

The composition of mappings is associative; that is, \((h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f)\).
If \(f\) and \(g\) are both one-to-one, then the mapping \(g\circ f\) is one-to-one.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are both onto, then the mapping \(g\circ f\) is onto.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are bijective, then so is \(g\circ f\).

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\circ)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\circ b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\circ b)\circ c=a\circ(b\circ c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\circ a=a\circ e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\circ a^{-1}=a^{-1}\circ a=e\).

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.10 — Uniqueness of Identity
The identity element in a group \(G\) is unique.

Suppose \(e\) and \(e'\) are both identity elements.
Since \(e\) is an identity, \(ee'=e'\).
Since \(e'\) is an identity, \(ee'=e\).
Therefore, \(e=ee'=e'\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.11 — Uniqueness of the Inverse
If \(g\) is any element in a group \(G\), then its inverse \(g^{-1}\) is unique.

Suppose \(g'\) and \(g''\) are both inverses of \(g\).
Then \(gg'=g'g=e\) and \(gg''=g''g=e\).
Therefore, \(g'=g'e=g'(gg'')=(g'g)g''=eg''=g''\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.12 — Inverse of a Product
Let \(G\) be a group. If \(a,b\in G\), then \((ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

Indeed,
\(abb^{-1}a^{-1}=aea^{-1}=aa^{-1}=e\),
and similarly,
\(b^{-1}a^{-1}ab=e\).
Thus \(b^{-1}a^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(ab\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.13 — Inverse of an Inverse
Let \(G\) be a group. For any \(a\in G\), \((a^{-1})^{-1}=a\).

Since
\(a^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=e\),
we obtain
\((a^{-1})^{-1}=e(a^{-1})^{-1}=aa^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=ae=a\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.14
Let \(G\) be a group and let \(a,b\in G\). Then the equations \(ax=b\) and \(xa=b\) have unique solutions in \(G\).

For \(ax=b\),
\(x=a^{-1}b\).
For \(xa=b\),
\(x=ba^{-1}\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.15
If \(G\) is a group and \(a,b,c\in G\), then
\(ba=ca\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\)
and
\(ab=ac\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\).

These are the right and left cancellation laws for groups.
For example,
\(ba=ca\quad\Longrightarrow\quad baa^{-1}=caa^{-1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\).

text:
Subgroups of \(\mathbb U(9)\) Continued
Consider \(\{[1],[5]\}\). \([5] \cdot [5]\) = [7], which is not in the set, so it is not a subgroup.

If we add [7] to the set, we get \(\{[1],[5],[7]\}\). \([5] \cdot [7]\) = [8], which is not in the set, so it is not a subgroup.


If we add [8] to the set, we get \(\{[1],[5],[7],[8]\}\). \([5] \cdot [7]\) = [8], which is in the set, but \([5] \cdot [8]\) = [4], which is not in the set, so it is not a subgroup.


If we add [4] to the set, we get \(\{[1],[4],[5],[7],[8]\}\). \([5] \cdot [7]\) = [8], which is in the set, but \([4] \cdot [5]\) = [2], which is not in the set, so it is not a subgroup.


If we add [2] to the set, we get \(\{[1],[2],[4],[5],[7],[8]\}\), which is \(\mathbb U(9)\), so it is a subgroup.

title: Slides: Definitions and Examples of Groups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\circ)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition \((a,b)\mapsto a\circ b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\circ b)\circ c=a\circ(b\circ c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\circ a=a\circ e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\circ a^{-1}=a^{-1}\circ a=e\).

title: Slides: Definitions and Examples of Groups
text:
Additional Definitions
A group is abelian (or commutative) if \(a\circ b=b\circ a\) for all \(a,b\in G\).
A Cayley table is a table that shows the result of the group operation for all pairs of elements in the group. We use it to verify that every element has an inverse. If the Caley table is symmetric about the diagonal, then the group is abelian.
The order of a group is the number of elements in the group. Groups can be finite or infinite.

Proposition 3.2.10 — Uniqueness of Identity
The identity element in a group \(G\) is unique.

Suppose \(e\) and \(e'\) are both identity elements.
Since \(e\) is an identity, \(ee'=e'\).
Since \(e'\) is an identity, \(ee'=e\).
Therefore, \(e=ee'=e'\).

Proposition 3.2.11 — Uniqueness of the Inverse
If \(g\) is any element in a group \(G\), then its inverse \(g^{-1}\) is unique.

Suppose \(g'\) and \(g''\) are both inverses of \(g\).
Then \(gg'=g'g=e\) and \(gg''=g''g=e\).
Therefore, \(g'=g'e=g'(gg'')=(g'g)g''=eg''=g''\).

Proposition 3.1.4.
Let \(\mathbb Z_n\) be the set of equivalence classes of the integers mod \(n\) and \(a,b,c \in \mathbb Z_n\).

Addition and multiplication are commutative:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a+b &\equiv b+a \pmod n \\
ab &\equiv ba \pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Addition and multiplication are associative:

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)+c &\equiv a+(b+c)\pmod n \\
(ab)c &\equiv a(bc)\pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Integer Equivalence Classes and Symmetries
text:
Proposition 3.1.4. Continued

There are both additive and multiplicative identities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a+0 &\equiv a \pmod n \\
a\cdot 1 &\equiv a \pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Multiplication distributes over addition:

\[
a(b+c)\equiv ab+ac\pmod n.
\]

text:

For every integer \(a\) there is an additive inverse \(-a\):

\[
a+(-a)\equiv 0\pmod n.
\]

Let \(a\) be a nonzero integer. Then \(\gcd(a,n)=1\) if and only if there exists a multiplicative inverse \(b\) for \(a\pmod n\); that is, a nonzero integer \(b\) such that

\[

Groups, rings, and fields! Oh My! These are the core algebraic structures in mathematics. Finally we get to the good stuff: axiomatic mathematics and discussing the rules and structures that are the baseline tools for all of mathematics. Groups, rings, and fields, the basic algebraic structures in contemporary mathematics.
